Athaliah seizes power; Jehoash becomes king (verses 1–12)

Athaliah tried to destroy everyone she knew to have a claim to the throne.

But one of the king's sons, Jehoash, was hidden.

God's promise to David now seemed to depend upon a single life, yet it did not fail.

Similarly, according to his promise, the Lord preserves a spiritual family for the Son of David.

His people may sometimes be hidden and unseen, but they are safe under God's protection.

Athaliah ruled tyrannically for six years before the rightful king was brought before the people.

He was only a child, but he had a good guardian—and, better still, the good God to whom he could turn.

We should welcome the reign of Christ within our own hearts with such joy and satisfaction.

Let Satan the usurper be cast out and the true King established upon his throne.

May Jesus live and reign forever in my soul and throughout the world.

Athaliah is put to death (verses 13–16)

Athaliah hurried toward her own ruin.

She was herself the greatest traitor, yet she was the first and loudest to cry out, “Treason! Treason!”

Those most deeply guilty are often the quickest to accuse others.

The worship of the Lord is restored (verses 17–21)

The king and people would be most faithfully united to one another when both were united to the Lord.

It is good for a nation when political changes help revive and strengthen true religion.

Solemn covenants remind us of duties that already bind us and strengthen our commitment to fulfill them.

The people immediately put an end to idolatry.

In accordance with their covenant, they also expressed their willingness to help one another.

The people rejoiced, and Jerusalem was peaceful.

The path to lasting joy and peace is wholehearted service to God.

Joy and thanksgiving are heard in the homes of the righteous, but there is no peace for the wicked.

Jehoash repairs the temple (verses 1–16)

It is a great kindness to young people, especially to those born into positions of influence, to have advisers who teach them to do what is right in the Lord's sight.

Those who are willing to receive good counsel act wisely.

The temple needed repairs, and Jehoash ordered them to be made.

The king showed zeal for the work.

God expects people with authority to use it in support of true worship, in correcting wrongs and repairing what has fallen into decay.

Jehoash first placed the priests in charge, expecting them to care deeply about the temple.

Yet little effective work was accomplished until the twenty-third year of his reign.

A different arrangement was then adopted.

When public funds are distributed faithfully, people become willing to contribute them generously.

Even while collecting what was needed to repair the temple, the people did not take away the priests' regular support.

Those serving in the temple must not be left hungry under the pretext of repairing its walls.

The people entrusted with the money handled their responsibilities carefully and honestly.

They did not buy ornaments until the necessary repairs were finished.

This teaches us to give priority to essential needs in our spending and to handle public money as carefully as our own.

Jehoash is killed by his servants (verses 17–21)

Consider Jehoash's character and the lessons his life offers.

His beginning was so promising, but the conclusion was deeply sorrowful.

It should prompt us to examine any decline in our own spiritual lives.

If we know Christ as the foundation of faith and hope, let us desire above all to know Christ.

May the work of the blessed Spirit be evident in our souls.

May we see and feel our need of Jesus and seek him earnestly in all the fullness and grace suited to us.

In this way our souls will turn away from dead works to serve the living and true God.

Chapter Outline

Verses 1-16
It is a great mercy to young people, especially to all young men of rank, like Jehoash, to have those about them who will instruct them to do what is right in the sight of the Lord; and they do wisely and well for themselves, when willing to be counselled and ruled. The temple was out of repair; Jehoash orders the repair of the temple. The king was zealous. God requires those who have power, to use it for the support of religion, the redress of grievances, and repairing of decays. The king employed the priests to manage, as most likely to be hearty in the work. But nothing was done effectually till the twenty-third year of his reign. Another method was therefore taken. When public distributions are made faithfully, public contributions will be made cheerfully. While they were getting all they could for the repair of the temple, they did not break in upon the stated maintenance of the priests. Let not the servants of the temple be starved, under colour of repairing the breaches of it. Those that were intrusted did the business carefully and faithfully. They did not lay it out in ornaments for the temple, till the other work was completed; hence we may learn, in all our expenses, to prefer that which is most needful, and, in dealing for the public, to deal as we would for ourselves.
[2Kgs.12.17-2Kgs.12.21]
Verses 17-21
Let us review the character of Jehoash, and consider what we may learn from it. When we see what a sad conclusion there was to so promising a beginning, it ought to make us seek into our spiritual declinings. If we know any thing of Christ as the foundation of our faith and hope, let us desire to know nothing but Christ. May the work of the blessed Spirit on our souls be manifest; may we see, feel, and be earnest, in seeking after Jesus in all his fulness, suitableness, and grace, that our souls may be brought over from dead works to serve the living and true God.

Jehoahaz rules Israel (verses 1–9)

In earlier times Israel had been honored as a people devoted to prayer.

In his distress, Jehoahaz appealed to the Lord for help.

He did not seek the help of the golden calves—what help could they offer?

He sought the living God.

Notice how quickly God shows mercy, how ready he is to hear prayer, and how willing to find a reason to act graciously.

Otherwise, he would not have appealed to the ancient covenant that Israel had broken and forfeited so many times.

This should draw us to him and encourage even those who have turned away to repent and return.

With the Lord there is forgiveness, so that he may be feared.

If he answers even a distressed person's request for temporary relief, how much more will he regard a prayer of faith for spiritual blessings!

Jehoash visits the dying Elisha (verses 10–19)

King Jehoash came to receive Elisha's last counsel and blessing.

There can be great spiritual benefit in visiting faithful believers during illness or near death.

The comfort they find in God as they die can strengthen our own faith.

Elisha promised the king success.

Yet Jehoash still had to seek God's direction and strength rather than rely entirely on his own hands.

The dying prophet's weak hands, signifying God's power, gave the arrow greater meaning and strength than the king's vigorous hands alone.

By treating the sign lightly, the king lost part of what it represented.

This grieved the dying prophet.

Good people are distressed when others reject blessings they could have received and lose opportunities for victory over spiritual enemies.

Elisha dies; Jehoash defeats Syria (verses 20–25)

God has many ways of correcting a people who have offended him.

Trouble may arrive from the direction least expected.

The invasion mentioned after Elisha's death suggests that losing faithful prophets can be a warning of coming judgment.

Elisha's dead body became the means by which another dead man was restored to life.

This miracle confirmed the truth of his prophecies.

It may also point toward Christ, through whose death and burial the grave has become a safe passage to life for every believer.

Jehoash defeated the Syrians as many times as he had struck the ground with the arrows.

Then his victories stopped.

Many people later regret the smallness of their faith and desires when it is too late to regain the blessings they neglected.

See how swift God is to show mercy; how ready to hear prayer; how willing to find a reason to be gracious; else he would not look so far back as the ancient covenant Israel had so often broken, and forfeited. Let this invite and engage us for ever to him; and encourage even those who have forsaken him, to return and repent; for there is forgiveness with him, that he may be feared. And if the Lord answer the mere cry of distress for temporal relief, much more will he regard the prayer of faith for spiritual blessings.
[2Kgs.13.10-2Kgs.13.19]

Jehoash, the king, came to Elisha, to receive his dying counsel and blessing. It may turn much to our spiritual advantage, to attend the sick-beds and death-beds of good men, that we may be encouraged in religion by the living comforts they have from it in a dying hour. Elisha assured the king of his success; yet he must look up to God for direction and strength; must reckon his own hands not enough, but go on, in dependence upon Divine aid. The trembling hands of the dying prophet, as they signified the power of God, gave this arrow more force than the hands of the king in his full strength. By contemning the sign, the king lost the thing signified, to the grief of the dying prophet. It is a trouble to good men, to see those to whom they wish well, forsake their own mercies, and to see them lose advantages against spiritual enemies.
[2Kgs.13.20-2Kgs.13.25]

God has many ways to chastise a provoking people. Trouble comes sometimes from that point whence we least feared it. The mention of this invasion on the death of Elisha, shows that the removal of God's faithful prophets is a presage of coming judgments. His dead body was a means of giving life to another dead body. This miracle was a confirmation of his prophecies. And it may have reference to Christ, by whose death and burial, the grave is made a safe and happy passage to life to all believers. Jehoash was successful against the Syrians, just as often as he had struck the ground with the arrows, then a stop was put to his victories. Many have repented, when too late, of distrusts and the straitness of their desires.

Amaziah begins well (verses 1–7)

Amaziah began his reign well but did not continue as he began.

It is not enough merely to repeat the good actions of faithful ancestors because those actions have become customary.

We must act from the same inward faith and devotion, with the same sincerity and determination that led them to do what was right.

Amaziah challenges Jehoash and loses (verses 8–14)

Soon after the kingdoms divided, Judah suffered greatly from Israel's hostility.

After Asa's time, Judah suffered still more from friendship and alliances with Israel.

Now hostility returned.

A humble person might almost smile to hear two proud and contemptuous rulers compete in belittling each other.

Unholy success produces pride.

Pride leads to conflict.

And proud people find the pride of others unbearable.

These tendencies cause trouble and sin in private life.

When they govern rulers, however, entire nations suffer.

Jehoash warned Amaziah about the folly of his challenge: “Your heart has made you proud.”

The root of every sin is in the heart.

Outward events, the circumstances Providence brings, or the opportunities we meet do not themselves make people proud, self-confident or discontented.

Such reactions come from the heart.

Amaziah is killed (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.15-2Kgs.14.22" resp="BibleResourcesOriginalSourceRangeInModernSectionHeading">verses 15–22</reference>)

Amaziah outlived the king who had defeated him by fifteen years.

He was later killed by his own subjects.

Azariah, also called Uzziah, appears to have been very young when his father died.

Henry understands his regnal years as counted from that event, although he thinks Azariah was not fully established as king until eleven years later.

This is Henry's chronological explanation, not an alteration of the biblical dates.

Jeroboam II's wicked reign (verses 23–29)

God raised up the prophet Jonah and through him announced merciful purposes toward Israel.

The continued presence of faithful ministers is a sign that God has not completely abandoned his people.

Henry gives two reasons why God granted Israel victories.

First, the people's suffering was so severe that they became objects of his compassion.

Second, the decree for their destruction had not yet been issued.

Israel had known many prophets.

But, according to Henry, none had left written prophetic books until this period.

Hosea began prophesying during Jeroboam's reign.

Amos was active around the same time; Micah came soon afterward, followed by Isaiah in the days of Ahaz and Hezekiah.

Even during the church's darkest and most corrupt periods, God raises up people who shine brightly.

Through their preaching and example they guide their own generation.

And through the writings of some of them, they continue to give light to later generations.

Amaziah began well, but did not go on so. It is not enough to do that which our pious predecessors did, merely to keep up the common usage, but we must do it as they did, from the same principle of faith and devotion, and with the same sincerity and resolution.

For some time after the division of the kingdoms, Judah suffered much from the enmity of Israel. After Asa's time, it suffered more by the friendship of Israel, and by the alliance made with them. Now we meet with hostility between them again. How may a humble man smile to hear two proud and scornful men set their wits on work, to vilify and undervalue one another! Unholy success excites pride; pride excites contentions. The effects of pride in others, are insufferable to those who are proud themselves. These are the sources of trouble and sin in private life; but when they arise between princes, they become the misery of their whole kingdoms. Jehoash shows Amaziah the folly of his challenge; Thine heart has lifted thee up. The root of all sin is in the heart, thence it flows. It is not Providence, the event, the occasion, whatever it is, that makes men proud, secure, discontented, or the like, but their own hearts do it. ( [2Kgs.14.15-2Kgs.14.22] 2Ki 14:15-22)
[2Kgs.14.15-2Kgs.14.22]
Verses 15-22
Amaziah survived his conqueror fifteen years. He was slain by his own subjects. Azariah, or Uzziah, seems to have been very young when his father was slain. Though the years of his reign are reckoned from that event, he was not fully made king till eleven years afterwards.
[2Kgs.14.23-2Kgs.14.29]
Verses 23-29
God raised up the prophet Jonah, and by him declared the purposes of his favour to Israel. It is a sign that God has not cast off his people, if he continues faithful ministers among them. Two reasons are given why God blessed them with those victories: 1. Because the distress was very great, which made them objects of his compassion. 2. Because the decree was not yet gone forth for their destruction. Many prophets there had been in Israel, but none left prophecies in writing till this age, and their prophecies are part of the Bible. Hosea began to prophesy in the reign of this Jeroboam. At the same time Amos prophesied; soon after Micah, then Isaiah, in the days of Ahaz and Hezekiah. Thus God, in the darkest and most degenerate ages of the church, raised up some to be burning and shining lights in it; to their own age, by their preaching and living, and a few by their writings, to reflect light upon us in the last times.

Azariah, also called Uzziah (verses 1–7)

Uzziah generally did what was right.

It was a blessing for Judah that a good reign lasted a long time.

Israel's later kings (verses 8–31)

This history shows how confused and troubled the kingdom of Israel had become.

Judah also suffered difficulties.

Yet compared with Israel, Judah's situation was a happy one.

The weaknesses that remain in genuine believers are very different from the deliberately permitted wickedness of people who do not fear God.

Such is our fallen human nature.

If our hearts were left entirely to themselves, they would prove deceitful above everything else and desperately wicked.

We have good reason to thank the Lord for restraints that have held us back from wrongdoing and for being kept away from temptation.

We should continually ask him to renew a right spirit within us.

Jotham rules Judah (verses 32–38)

Jotham showed great respect for the temple.

Rulers may not be able to accomplish everything they wish in restraining vice and irreverence.

When that happens, they should work all the more diligently to support and encourage godliness and moral virtue.

Ahaz's wicked reign (verses 1–9)

Ahaz's days were few and filled with evil.

Those whose own consciences condemn them will turn almost anywhere for help in trouble rather than turn to God.

His sin became its own punishment.

It is common for people to try to escape the difficulties created by one sin through committing another.

Ahaz copies a foreign altar (verses 10–16)

Until this time God's altar had remained in its appointed place and had been used for worship.

Ahaz replaced it with another.

Human beings have a natural inclination toward some form of religion, and that inclination is not easily extinguished.

But unless it is governed by God's word and Spirit, it can produce foolish superstition or detestable idolatry.

At best, it may quiet a guilty conscience through meaningless ceremonies.

People who reject true faith have often been especially willing to believe ridiculous falsehoods.

Ahaz damages the temple (verses 17–20)

Ahaz treated the Sabbath with contempt, opening the way for many other sins.

He did this to please the king of Assyria.

People who once had ready access to the Lord's house but turn away from it to please their neighbors are rapidly moving toward ruin.

Hoshea and Israel's exile (verses 1–6)

When sin reaches its full measure, the Lord no longer delays judgment.

Samaria's inhabitants must have suffered terribly.

Some poor Israelites remained in the land.

Most of those carried into distant exile were absorbed among the other nations.

Why Israel was taken captive (verses 7–23)

The destruction of Israel's northern kingdom is reported briefly, but these verses explain its causes in detail.

The ruin came from the Almighty.

Assyria was only the rod of his anger (Isaiah 10:5).

Those who bring sin into a country or household bring disaster with it and must answer for the suffering that follows.

The world's outward acts of wrongdoing are enormous.

Yet even greater are the hidden sins of the human heart—evil thoughts, desires and intentions.

Some public sins carry obvious disgrace.

But ingratitude toward God, neglect of him, hostility to him, idolatry and the ungodliness arising from them are even more deeply malignant.

No one possesses genuine godliness without turning from every evil path and keeping God's commands.

But such obedience must grow out of faith in God's testimony concerning his anger against all unrighteousness and his mercy in Jesus Christ.

The peoples settled in Israel (verses 24–41)

The terror of divine judgment can produce forced or feigned submission in people whose hearts remain unconverted.

This happened among the foreigners brought to settle in Israel.

Such people hold unworthy views of God.

They expect outward religious forms to satisfy him.

They also attempt the impossible task of combining his service with love of the world and indulgence of sinful desires.

May the fear of the Lord, which begins true wisdom, take hold of our hearts and direct our conduct.

Then we will be prepared for whatever change life brings.

Earthly homes and settlements are uncertain.

We do not know where we may be driven before death, and in any case we must soon leave this world.

But the righteous have chosen the good portion that will never be taken away.

Hezekiah's good reign and removal of idolatry (verses 1–8)

Hezekiah was a true son of David.

Other kings had done what was right, but had not followed David's example as closely.

We must not assume that when times and people become bad, matters must inevitably grow worse.

After many evil kings, God raised up someone who resembled David himself.

The bronze serpent had been carefully preserved as a memorial of God's kindness to Israel in the wilderness.

Yet burning incense to it was foolish and wicked.

Attempts to help worship by means not authorized in Scripture interrupt the exercise of faith and lead toward superstition and other serious evils.

Fallen human nature corrupts such practices.

True faith has no need of these artificial aids.

God's word, considered daily and accompanied by prayer, provides all the outward assistance needed.

Sennacherib attacks Judah (verses 9–16)

Sennacherib's invasion brought great suffering upon Judah.

Through it, God tested Hezekiah's faith and corrected the people.

Hidden unbelief, hypocrisy and spiritual lukewarmness among many required correction.

For sincere believers, such trials purify faith and hope and lead to simple dependence upon God.

Rabshakeh speaks against the Lord (verses 17–37)

Rabshakeh tried to persuade Judah that resistance was pointless.

He asked, “What is this confidence you are trusting?”

How good it would be if sinners applied a similar question to themselves and sought peace with God!

It is wise to submit to the Lord because resistance against him cannot succeed.

What basis for confidence do people have when they stubbornly oppose him?

Rabshakeh's speech was clever and carefully constructed.

Yet it was full of pride, malice, falsehood and blasphemy.

Hezekiah's officers remained silent.

There is a time to remain silent as well as a time to speak.

Some people are so determined to mock what is holy or reject reason that presenting religious truths to them is like throwing pearls before pigs.

Their silence made Rabshakeh even prouder and more confident.

Sometimes the wisest response is to let people continue their insults rather than argue.

A firm expression of abhorrence can be sufficient witness against such behavior.

We must leave the whole matter with the Lord, who holds every heart in his hands, entrusting ourselves to him with humility, hope and earnest prayer.

Verses 1-8
Hezekiah was a true son of David. Some others did that which was right, but not like David. Let us not suppose that when times and men are bad, they must needs grow worse and worse; that does not follow: after many bad kings, God raised one up like David himself. The brazen serpent had been carefully preserved, as a memorial of God's goodness to their fathers in the wilderness; but it was idle and wicked to burn incense to it. All helps to devotion, not warranted by the word of God, interrupt the exercise of faith; they always lead to superstition and other dangerous evils. Human nature perverts every thing of this kind. True faith needs not such aids; the word of God, daily thought upon and prayed over, is all the outward help we need.
[2Kgs.18.9-2Kgs.18.16]
Verses 9-16
The descent Sennacherib made upon Judah, was a great calamity to that kingdom, by which God would try the faith of Hezekiah, and chastise the people. The secret dislike, the hypocrisy, and lukewarmness of numbers, require correction; such trials purify the faith and hope of the upright, and bring them to simple dependence on God.
[2Kgs.18.17-2Kgs.18.37]
Verses 17-37
Rabshakeh tries to convince the Jews, that it was to no purpose for them to stand it out. What confidence is this wherein thou trustest? It were well if sinners would submit to the force of this argument, in seeking peace with God. It is, therefore, our wisdom to yield to him, because it is in vain to contend with him: what confidence is that which those trust in who stand out against him? A great deal of art there is in this speech of Rabshakeh; but a great deal of pride, malice, falsehood, and blasphemy. Hezekiah's nobles held their peace. There is a time to keep silence, as well as a time to speak; and there are those to whom to offer any thing religious or rational, is to cast pearls before swine. Their silence made Rabshakeh yet more proud and secure. It is often best to leave such persons to rail and blaspheme; a decided expression of abhorrence is the best testimony against them. The matter must be left to the Lord, who has all hearts in his hands, committing ourselves unto him in humble submission, believing hope, and fervent prayer.

Hezekiah hears a message of reassurance (verses 1–7)

Hezekiah was deeply troubled by the dishonor Rabshakeh's blasphemy brought upon God.

When we receive God's word through his messengers, we should especially desire that they pray to God for us.

The great Prophet is also our great Intercessor.

People who lift their hearts to the Lord in prayer may expect his help.

Human desperation provides a special occasion for God to show his power.

While the Lord's servants must announce warnings to the irreverent, proud and hypocritical, they also bring words of comfort to discouraged believers.

Sennacherib's letter and Hezekiah's prayer (verses 8–19)

Prayer is an unfailing refuge for Christians facing temptation, whether the struggle comes from outward troubles or inward enemies.

At the mercy seat of our all-powerful Friend, we may open our hearts and lay our problems before him, as Hezekiah spread out the letter.

We may appeal confidently to his mercy.

When we recognize that God's glory is involved in our cause, faith receives fresh strength and rejoices that it will not be shaken.

Our strongest reasons for asking God's help are those drawn from his own honor.

God foretells Sennacherib's defeat (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.20-2Kgs.19.34" resp="BibleResourcesOriginalSourceRangeInModernSectionHeading">verses 20–34</reference>)

Every movement of Sennacherib was known to God.

The Lord himself promised to defend the city.

Any person or place he has undertaken to protect is secure.

The Assyrian invasion probably prevented Judah's fields from being sown that year.

Henry supposes that the following year was a Sabbath year.

Yet God promised enough food from the land to sustain the people through those two years.

This provision would follow the destruction of Sennacherib's army.

The future harvest therefore served as a sign to strengthen Hezekiah's present faith, assuring him that the promised deliverance would come and that the Lord would continue caring for Judah.

God promised these things not because the people deserved them but for his own glory.

May our hearts be good soil in which his word takes root and bears fruit through our lives.

The Assyrian army is destroyed (verses 35–37)

That very night, after God's message reached Hezekiah, the greater part of the Assyrian army was killed.

See how weak even the strongest people are before Almighty God!

Who has hardened himself against the Lord and prospered?

Sennacherib's own sons later murdered him.

Parents who suffer from disobedient children should ask whether they themselves have disobeyed their Father in heaven.

This history powerfully confirms the value of steadfast trust in God.

He may afflict his people, but he will not abandon them.

It is good when troubles drive us to prayer.

Yet our dependence on emergencies may also expose our unbelief.

How reluctant we are to rest entirely on God's promises!

How eagerly we want to know how he will save us!

How impatient we become when relief is delayed!

We must wait for his word to be fulfilled.

Lord, help our unbelief!

At the mercy-seat of his almighty Friend he opens his heart, spreads his case, like Hezekiah, and makes his appeal. When he can discern that the glory of God is engaged on his side, faith gains the victory, and he rejoices that he shall never be moved. The best pleas in prayer are taken from God's honour. Verses 20-34
All Sennacherib's motions were under the Divine cognizance. God himself undertakes to defend the city; and that person, that place, cannot but be safe, which he undertakes to protect. The invasion of the Assyrians probably had prevented the land from being sown that year. The next is supposed to have been the sabbatical year, but the Lord engaged that the produce of the land should be sufficient for their support during those two years. As the performance of this promise was to be after the destruction of Sennacherib's army, it was a sign to Hezekiah's faith, assuring him of that present deliverance, as an earnest of the Lord's future care of the kingdom of Judah. This the Lord would perform, not for their righteousness, but his own glory. May our hearts be as good ground, that his word may strike root therein, and bring forth fruit in our lives.

That night which followed the sending of this message to Hezekiah, the main body of their army was slain. See how weak the mightiest men are before Almighty God. Who ever hardened himself against Him and prospered? The king of Assyria's own sons became his murderers. Those whose children are undutiful, ought to consider whether they have not been so to their Father in heaven? This history exhibits a strong proof of the good of firm trust and confidence in God. He will afflict, but not forsake his people. It is well when our troubles drive us to our knees. But does it not reprove our unbelief? How unwilling are we to rest on the declaration of Jehovah! How desirous to know in what way he will save us! How impatient when relief is delayed! But we must wait for the fulfilling of his word. Lord, help our unbelief.

Hezekiah becomes ill and recovers (verses 1–11)

Hezekiah became gravely ill, close to death, in the same year that the king of Assyria besieged Jerusalem.

Isaiah brought him a warning to prepare for death.

Prayer is one of the best ways to prepare for death.

Through prayer we receive grace and strength from God to finish life well.

Hezekiah wept bitterly.

Some understand this as an unwillingness to die, and it is natural for human beings to dread the separation of body and soul.

But Hezekiah's circumstances were special.

He was in the midst of useful service.

His prayer, recorded also in Isaiah 38, helps us understand his tears.

Nothing in it suggests that he was tormented by the enslaving fear of death.

His devotion to God made his sickbed easier to bear.

He prayed, “Lord, remember me.”

He did not imply that God needed reminding, or that he could demand a reward as something owed to him.

Only Christ's righteousness has purchased mercy and grace.

Hezekiah did not simply pray, “Spare my life.”

He prayed that God would remember him.

Whether he lived or died, he wanted to belong to the Lord.

God always hears the prayers of the brokenhearted.

He grants health, longer life and earthly deliverance for as long as those gifts are truly good for his people.

Hezekiah was instructed to use means of recovery.

Yet his disease was so advanced, and the change so sudden, that his healing was miraculous.

When ill, we should use appropriate treatments that support the body's natural healing.

Refusing such help does not display faith in God; it tests him.

To confirm Hezekiah's faith, God caused the sun's shadow to move backward, miraculously lengthening the period of light.

The sign showed the Lord's power in heaven as well as on earth, his attention to prayer and his kindness toward those he has chosen.

Hezekiah displays his wealth (verses 12–21)

At that time the king of Babylon was independent of Assyria, though he would soon be conquered by it.

Hezekiah proudly showed the visitors his treasures, weapons and other evidence of wealth and power.

This revealed pride, love of display and a departure from simple trust in God.

It also seems he missed an opportunity to tell the Babylonian visitors about the Lord who had performed the miracles that interested them and to explain why idolatry was foolish and wrong.

Showing visitors our homes and possessions is not wrong in itself.

But when we display them because we want praise for ourselves while withholding glory from God, it becomes sin, as it did for Hezekiah.

We may expect trouble from anything in which we take excessive pride.

Isaiah had often comforted Hezekiah.

Now he came to correct him.

The blessed Spirit is likewise both Comforter and Reprover (John 16:7–8).

Ministers must fulfill both roles when needed.

Hezekiah acknowledged the justice of God's sentence and his goodness in delaying it.

Yet the announcement of what would happen to his family and nation must have been painful.

Hezekiah had truly been humbled for his pride.

Blessed are those who die in the Lord: they rest from their work, and their deeds follow them.

Verses 1-11
Hezekiah was sick unto death, in the same year in which the king of Assyria besieged Jerusalem. A warning to prepare for death was brought to Hezekiah by Isaiah. Prayer is one of the best preparations for death, because by it we fetch in strength and grace from God, to enable us to finish well. He wept sorely: some gather from hence that he was unwilling to die; it is in the nature of man to dread the separation of soul and body. There was also something peculiar in Hezekiah's case; he was now in the midst of his usefulness. Let Hezekiah's prayer, see Is 38. interpret his tears; in that is nothing which is like his having been under that fear of death, which has bondage or torment. Hezekiah's piety made his sick-bed easy. "O Lord, remember now;" he does not speak as if God needed to be put in mind of any thing by us; nor, as if the reward might be demanded as due; it is Christ's righteousness only that is the purchase of mercy and grace. Hezekiah does not pray, Lord, spare me; but, Lord, remember me; whether I live or die, let me be thine. God always hears the prayers of the broken in heart, and will give health, length of days, and temporal deliverances, as much and as long as is truly good for them. Means were to be used for Hezekiah's recovery; yet, considering to what a height the disease was come, and how suddenly it was checked, the cure was miraculous. It is our duty, when sick, to use such means as are proper to help nature, else we do not trust God, but tempt him. For the confirmation of his faith, the shadow of the sun was carried back, and the light was continued longer than usual, in a miraculous manner. This work of wonder shows the power of God in heaven as well as on earth, the great notice he takes of prayer, and the great favour he bears to his chosen.
[2Kgs.20.12-2Kgs.20.21]
Verses 12-21
The king of Babylon was at this time independent of the king of Assyria, though shortly after subdued by him. Hezekiah showed his treasures and armour, and other proofs of his wealth and power. This was the effect of pride and ostentation, and departing from simple reliance on God. He also seems to have missed the opportunity of speaking to the Chaldeans, about Him who had wrought the miracles which excited their attention, and of pointing out to them the absurdity and evil of idolatry. What is more common than to show our friends our houses and possessions? But if we do this in the pride of ours hearts, to gain applause from men, not giving praise to God, it becomes sin in us, as it did in Hezekiah. We may expect vexation from every object with which we are unduly pleased. Isaiah, who had often been Hezekiah's comforter, is now is reprover. The blessed Spirit is both, [John.16.7] Joh 16:7, [John.16.8] 8. Ministers must be both, as there is occasion. Hezekiah allowed the justice of the sentence, and God's goodness in the respite. Yet the prospect respecting his family and nation must have given him many painful feelings. Hezekiah was indeed humbled for the pride of his heart. And blessed are the dead who die in the Lord; for they rest from their labours, and their works do follow them.
